title: Air India Crash Probe Enters Final Stages With Cockpit Recorder Transcript Ready
excerpt: India's AAIB has completed a psychological autopsy and cockpit voice recorder transcript as the investigation into the Boeing 787 disaster that killed 260 nears conclusion, with a draft final report expected by October.
body:
• India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has prepared a cockpit voice recorder transcript and conducted a psychological autopsy in the Air India crash probe.
  • The investigation is now in its analysis phase, with remaining work expected to wrap up within six weeks and a draft final report due around October 2026.
  • Captain's father Pushkar Raj Sabharwal filed a lawsuit after investigators allegedly implied his son cut fuel to the engines; AAIB says media speculation has made witnesses uncooperative.
  • The crash on June 12, 2025 killed 260 people — 241 on board and 19 on the ground — making it the deadliest aviation disaster in a decade.

Investigation Milestones

More than a year after a Boeing 787 Dreamliner crashed shortly after takeoff from Ahmedabad, killing 260 people, India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) has entered the final stages of its probe, according to a court filing dated July 15, 2026.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=F6xFALc03CQ

The AAIB has completed two critical milestones: a full transcript of the cockpit voice recorder and a psychological autopsy, though it did not identify whose autopsy was conducted or disclose findings from either, according to Reuters. An analysis of data retrieved in late May from an engine monitoring unit remains pending, and an assessment of organisational factors is still in progress.

Investigators have interviewed Air India 787 pilots, crew members who had previously flown with the crashed aircraft's pilots, technical personnel involved in preparing the jet, air traffic controllers, weather officials and human-factors specialists, the AAIB said.

What Happened in the Cockpit

Air India Flight 171, a Boeing 787 Dreamliner registered as VT-ANB, was operating from Ahmedabad to London on June 12, 2025. The aircraft lifted off at 08:08:39 GMT and reached a maximum airspeed of 180 knots three seconds later.

"Immediately thereafter, the Engine 1 and Engine 2 fuel cutoff switches transitioned from RUN to CUTOFF position one after another with a time gap of 01 sec."

— India's preliminary investigation report

The cockpit voice recording captured one pilot asking the other why he cut off the fuel. The other pilot responded that he did not do so. CCTV footage from the airport showed the Ram Air Turbine deploying during the initial climb, an emergency measure that activates when engines lose power. The aircraft began losing altitude before it even crossed the airport perimeter wall.

Both fuel cutoff switches were moved back to the RUN position within 14 seconds, but only Engine 1 showed signs of recovery. Engine 2 relit but could not arrest its deceleration. One pilot transmitted "MAYDAY MAYDAY MAYDAY" at 08:09:05 GMT. Data recording stopped six seconds later.

The aircraft struck a college hostel building. Of the 242 people on board — 230 passengers and 12 crew — only one survived: Vishwash Kumar Ramesh, 40, a British citizen seated near an emergency exit. Nineteen people on the ground were also killed.

Legal Battle and Witness Problems

The court filing that revealed these investigation details came about through a lawsuit filed by Pushkar Raj Sabharwal, father of Captain Sumeet Sabharwal, who had 15,638 flying hours including 8,596 on the Boeing 787. The elder Sabharwal said AAIB officials who visited his home implied his son deliberately cut fuel to the engines after takeoff.

U.S. officials' early assessment, reported by Reuters last year, supported the view that the captain cut the flow of fuel. The AAIB responded at the time that it was "too early to reach any definite conclusions."

The AAIB acknowledged in its filing that media speculation and narratives attributing blame to the pilots had caused some witnesses to become "restrictive and non-responsive" — a significant complication for a probe of this magnitude.

Impact on Aviation Safety

The crash — the world's deadliest aviation disaster in a decade — triggered immediate action across the industry. India and South Korea ordered airlines to check fuel switches on several Boeing models. Singapore Airlines made precautionary checks. The U.S. FAA and Boeing privately issued notifications that the fuel switch locks on their aircraft were safe.

For Air India, which Tata Group acquired in 2022 and has been positioning as a "world-class airline," the disaster represented a severe setback. Air India and its low-cost unit have faced intense scrutiny from India's aviation regulator over maintenance lapses since the crash. Flying anxiety spiked across India, with some travellers becoming more selective about their airline and aircraft choices.

What's Next

The AAIB expects remaining investigation activities to be completed within about six weeks, subject to "external dependencies." A draft final report is anticipated around October 2026, after which it will be circulated to participating countries — including to the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board — for comments before being finalised and published.

Among the 260 dead were 169 Indians, 53 Britons, 7 Portuguese nationals and 1 Canadian — a cross-section of the diaspora that routinely uses Air India for long-haul routes between India and Europe. Families continue to press for accountability and closure, more than 13 months after the disaster.
